THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE 97

With a mental perspective adjusted to these conditions one can more readily reconcile himself to the picture of a Savoy College boy living on a neighboring farm and trekking a distance of several miles—no item in those days—to the College with his well-filled dinner pail swinging in one hand and a heavy stack of books under the other arm. Or perhaps the young man, or even a young lady, rode horseback, the latter picturesquely perched on a side-saddle and wearing a long, black, bundlesome riding skirt, which of course was taken off before she went into the schoolroom. (A stile block, to assist young ladies in dismounting and mounting, stood on the edge of the campus.)

Again, the student may have ridden to school in a horse-drawn buggy or phaeton. In either case, there was a horse to be unsaddled or unharnessed and tied to a tree in the woods bordering the campus. At noon there was the horse to be fed and watered before the student could eat his own lunch; and in the afternoon there was the matter of saddling or harnessing the animal for the homeward ride.

Life in the bachelor halls had its own separate routine, of course. The following poem by an early student may serve to complete this description and indicate the nature of undergraduate literary efforts of the early Savoy days. It was sent to The Platonian Messenger by Mr. E. F. Adams, from Kingston, Texas, April 10, with a note stating that it was written by Mr. J. C. Kyger, in 1878, and read by Mr. W. W.
